concept: Individual Buyer Best Practices at Salvage Auctions
summary: Depth-first rabbithole dossier for Individual Buyer Best Practices at Salvage Auctions; source-anchored research pack.

facts.text: **U-1. Is a broker a protection or a liability for an individual buyer?** Sources framing broker use as best practice emphasize access and bidding expertise (<https://www.carproxy.com/how-it-works/preview-copart-vehicles>), while the retitling literature requires the salvage title, parts receipts, and bill of sale to be in one and the same name (<https://carregistrationfee.com/articles/salvage-rebuilt-title-registration.html>). Whether a broker-mediated purchase satisfies that name-matching test, and under which states' rules, is not resolved by any source found. **This is the single most cons

This report covers what an *individual, non-dealer buyer* must do to buy safely and legally at a salvage auto auction in the United States: gaining access to the auction, checking title and brand history before bidding, inspecting the vehicle and its safety-critical repaired parts, and retitling the vehicle after purchase. It traces how individual access to salvage auctions came about, and identifies the primary and official sources that govern each step.

- **How many states actually let an individual bid on a salvage vehicle.** Secondary sources give specific counts — one commercial blog claims roughly 28 states require a licensed broker for private buyers of salvage vehicles. No official or primary source was found that enumerates this nationally; the only verified state-level rule in this run is Wisconsin's, which forbids personal purchases on a BID card. The national count is therefore **unverified** and should not be treated as fact. NMVTIS and the Copart 10-K both confirm the underlying structure (state-by-state regulation), not the tally

48. The FTC Used Car Rule's Buyers Guide requirement, which is the main federal disclosure protection in retail used-car buying, does not apply here in either of the two ways that matter: "The Rule does not apply at auctions that are closed to consumers," and excepted from the Rule is "any vehicle sold for scrap or parts if the dealer submits title documents to the appropriate state authority and obtains a salvage certification" — https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/dealers-guide-used-car-rule. 49. Where the Rule *does* apply (a public auction open to consumers), the Buyers Guide i

4. By FY2025 the general public is a named, standing segment of the buyer base, and the license requirement has been narrowed to business members only. Copart's FY2025 Form 10-K describes "approximately 1 million registered members ('buyers') in the vehicle dismantling and recycling, rebuilding, used vehicle dealer and export industries, as well as members that are a part of the general public," and states: "To become a registered member, a person or business must complete a basic application either online or through our mobile application. Before any member may purchase a vehicle, they must p

12. For flood-exposed salvage, the FTC's published buyer checklist (January 11, 2018) is the canonical consumer-facing source: "Have your mechanic inspect the car's mechanical and electrical components, and systems that contain fluids, for water contamination"; look for "water stains, mildew, sand, or silt under the carpet, floor mats, and dashboard"; look for "fogging inside the headlights and taillights"; treat "a heavy aroma of cleaners and disinfectants" as a masking signal. The FTC defines a flood title as damage "from sitting in water deep enough to fill the engine compartment" and a sal

15. California's inspection is a theft-and-identity inspection, not only a safety inspection, and it requires paperwork the buyer must collect *at the time of purchase*. Under the CHP Salvage Vehicle Inspection Program, authorized by California Vehicle Code § 5505 and established by SB 1713, applicants must present "bills of sale or invoices for the vehicle and any replaced component parts," and officers verify that "identification numbers have not been removed, falsified, altered, defaced, destroyed, or tampered with" and that "there are no indications the vehicle or any of its component part

**C4. Buying through a broker imports a home-state registration restriction that defeats the usual reason to buy.** A Copart-hosted broker's buyer terms (dated 04.22.2024) state: "Any Buyer, regardless of state of residence, is unable to purchase vehicles in their home state with the intent to register the vehicle in their home state," with exclusions for parts use, export, an active dealer licence in that state, or out-of-state registration. The same document separately declines to assist Florida, California, and Washington residents buying in those states for in-state registration. An indivi

**C11. Run an NMVTIS-sourced history report before bidding, because brand history is permanent and federally sourced.** NMVTIS lets a buyer see "information from a vehicle's current title, including the vehicle's brand history," the latest reported odometer readings, insurer determinations of "salvage" or "total loss," and reports of transfer to auto recyclers, junkyards, or salvage yards. Once a state brands a vehicle, "that brand becomes a permanent part of the vehicle's NMVTIS record." NMVTIS is "the only vehicle-history database in the nation to which all states, insurance carriers, and ju
*Best practice implied:* keep the auction invoice and every parts receipt from day one. In California, missing parts receipts stop the retitling, not just the repair.

**C12. ⚠ A clean NMVTIS report is weak evidence, not clearance.** The programme's own consumer page states the report is "intentionally concise," that not all states currently report data, that a "clean" report "could yield a false negative if prior states didn't report," that state standards vary so "a vehicle's junk yard history doesn't guarantee a junk brand," and that the report "doesn't contain all information in a state's full title record." A buyer who treats a clean NMVTIS result as a pass is over-reading the instrument.

**C15. Safety-critical inspection of a salvage or rebuilt vehicle is specifically urged by NHTSA because of substandard replacement airbag inflators.** NHTSA reports that eleven people have died and three were severely injured in fourteen crashes involving replacement air bag inflators "likely illegally imported into the United States," that most known crashes involved vehicles "mostly with salvage or rebuilt titles," and that "if a vehicle has a salvage or rebuilt title, it is especially urgent that it be inspected for one of these inflators." Practice: treat any prior airbag deployment as re

**C19. Re-titling requires passing state safety and anti-theft inspection, and the resulting title stays branded.** In Texas, "a rebuilt vehicle must pass safety and anti-theft inspections, and other state-mandated standards in order to return to the road," a new inspection is required regardless of whether repairs were made, and "your Texas title will include the 'Rebuilt Salvage' brand." Newly assembled vehicles or those using component parts additionally require an ASE Certified Master Technician inspection on Form VTR-64 (or VTR-852). Budget the inspection and the residual brand into the p

This report covers **only** the practices an *individual, non-dealer* buyer follows when bidding at a salvage auction (Copart, IAA, and comparable insurance/total-loss auctions), and where those practices break down. It deliberately stays inside that boundary: it does not cover dealer-only wholesale auctions, general used-car buying, salvage-vehicle economics for rebuilders as a business, or the parent domain's other branches. Those are separate frontier items.

**G-3.** Overbidding is amplified specifically when **quality uncertainty is high**: bidders overbid not only from inexperience and auction fever but because they overestimate the item's value under uncertainty. Salvage auctions maximize quality uncertainty by construction (**B-1**–**B-3**), so this is the worst environment for a first-time bidder, not merely a cheap one. <http://ojs.jecr.org/jecr/sites/default/files/paper3_1.doc>

6. Registering with the auction operator does not by itself make an individual eligible to buy a salvage vehicle. Copart's FY2025 10-K states: "The acquisition and sale of vehicles is regulated by various state, provincial and foreign motor vehicle departments, and the steps required to process vehicle titles is a significant cost of our business." (https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/900075/000162828025042946/cprt-20250731.htm)

**C-3.** *The converse trap.* Possession by a junk or salvage yard does not obligate a state to brand the vehicle, and states differ on the damage threshold that triggers a salvage designation. So an unbranded title is compatible with severe, documented damage. <https://vehiclehistory.bja.ojp.gov/nmvtis_consumers>
**Geography.** United States. Copart and IAA (Insurance Auto Auctions, RB Global) are used as the reference platforms because they handle the bulk of US insurance total-loss volume.

33. Payment is due on a short, fixed clock. Copart's member guide: "Pay for your vehicle within three (3) business days, including the sale date. Payment must include any applicable fees and sales tax" — https://www.copart.ca/content/us/en-ca/pdfs/newmemberguide_en.pdf (p. 12). 34. A broker may impose a *tighter* clock than the auction: the PAB agreement requires payment "within 2 working days (auction day plus 1 working day…)" with a $50/unit late fee — https://www.copart.com/content/us/en/pdfs/terms%20&%20conditions_01082020.pdf (p. 2). 35. Payment method affects cost and speed: Copart class

**C5. Bidding capacity is capped by a security deposit at roughly a 10:1 ratio, so the deposit sets the buyer's practical price ceiling.** The same broker terms require "a minimum of $600.00 USD on deposit to be able to buy," state that the $600 deposit "shall be sufficient to enable a buyer to be the high bidder on one single vehicle for up to $6,000.00 USD," and require an additional "$100.00 USD for each additional $1,000.00 USD of desired bid." Each simultaneous vehicle needs its own $600 minimum deposit. Practice: fund the deposit to the intended ceiling days before the sale, because the

**C24. Federal reporting exists specifically because undisclosed salvage history is a known fraud vector.** DOJ/OJP states NMVTIS is designed so that consumers can "detect fraud and determine whether a car has been totaled or classified as salvage or junk," and that federal law mandates all insurance companies and junk/salvage yards nationwide report their salvage and total-loss vehicles.

5. Remote bidding is now the norm, not the exception, which is why an individual buyer's inspection and transport planning matter more than they did at a live sale. In FY2025, "sales of U.S. vehicles, on a unit basis, to members registered outside the state where the vehicle was located accounted for 69.8% of total vehicles sold; of which 31.0% of vehicles were sold to out of state members within the U.S. and 38.8% were sold to International members." The comparable FY2004 figure was 41%. (https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/900075/000162828025042946/cprt-20250731.htm ; https://www.sec.gov

1. **What counts as a "safe" bid ceiling has no authoritative source.** A commonly repeated practitioner rule caps total landed cost at 50–70% of after-repair value, but every instance found was a commercial broker, transport, or content-marketing site, not a primary or standards source. No government, insurer, or peer-reviewed source was located that quantifies a defensible bid ceiling for individual buyers. Treat the figure as folklore until sourced.

2. **Total-loss threshold and salvage-branding thresholds are routinely conflated, including in secondary sources.** The MWL chart states plainly that the two are "different but related concepts … often conflated" and that threshold laws "do not bind insurance companies." Popular comparison sites nonetheless present state percentages (ranges quoted variously as 60%–100%) as if they determined whether a given vehicle is salvage. The percentages in circulation could not be verified against a primary statutory source within this run, and the 2021-12-15 chart date means individual state figures ma

- **Whether salvage-auction buying is economically sound for an individual.** Sought as a disconfirming line of evidence. No primary or official source was found that quantifies it. The available material is commercial and unreliable: insurance-comparison sites claim rebuilt-title vehicles resell for 20–50% below clean-title comparables and that full coverage is often unavailable or 20–40% more expensive. These figures are **not** sourced to any insurer filing, regulator, or study, and are recorded here only to mark that the disconfirming case exists and remains unevidenced. This is the larges

**Verdict: `BUDGET_EXHAUSTED` (soft stop), not depth saturation.** The rate is declining steeply but has not hit the two-consecutive-passes-under-5% threshold. The brief asked for a concise report, so the loop was stopped at Pass 3. Two further passes look likely to still pay off: (1) recovering current primary fee schedules and the exact IAA auction rules text (§3.4, §3.5); (2) a state-law pass establishing a dated, cited list of which states permit direct private salvage purchase (§3.2).

**C8. Payment windows are measured in working days and storage penalties escalate, so transport must be arranged before bidding, not after winning.** Payments are "due within 2 working days (not including auction day)"; unremoved vehicles incur storage "starting at $5 USD per day, and upwards of $30 USD per day, after 10 days"; a vehicle not removed after 20 calendar days may be resold to cover storage, and after 30 calendar days becomes subject to abandonment. Non-payment within seven calendar days forfeits the security deposit and exposes the buyer to a relist fee of "$600.00 to $1,000.00 or

**C13. ⚠ A clean title at a salvage auction does not mean the vehicle was not a total loss.** State total-loss thresholds bind title branding, not insurer claim decisions: "the total threshold laws do not bind insurance companies adjusting auto property loss claims. For example, in a state with an 80% salvage title threshold, a vehicle's repairs may be at 75% of market value, but the carrier … declares the vehicle to be a total loss. In such an instance, the vehicle could go to the salvage auction as a total loss, yet it would retain a clean title under state law." The same reference notes tha

**E-4.** *Name-matching constraint.* The salvage title, the parts and repair receipts, and the bill of sale or total-loss settlement letter must all be in the same name. An individual who buys through a broker, or who has a shop buy parts on the shop's account, can fail this test on paperwork alone even with a sound vehicle. This interacts directly with the broker requirement in **A-2** and is a plausible mechanism by which the two "best practices" conflict. <https://carregistrationfee.com/articles/salvage-rebuilt-title-registration.html> **[secondary — mechanism inferred from the stated name-

This report covers only the operational practices available to a **private individual** (not a licensed dealer, dismantler, or rebuilder) bidding at **salvage / total-loss vehicle auctions** in the United States — chiefly Copart and IAA. It covers eligibility, the fee and deposit mechanics that determine landed cost, pre-bid evaluation methods, the post-purchase titling path, and the known failure modes. It does **not** cover wholesale dealer-only auctions, retail used-car buying, repossession or government-fleet sales, or the insurer-side total-loss decision except where that decision changes

7. At least one state bars individuals from salvage-pool bidding outright, and bars licensed buyers from buying for themselves. Wisconsin DOT: a Salvage Buyer Identification (BID) card is available only to "a licensed dealer, wholesaler or salvage dealer or their employee," it permits bidding "at motor vehicle salvage pools (auctions that sell salvage vehicles only)," and "BID card users can only buy vehicles on behalf of their employer. BID card users cannot buy vehicles for personal use." (https://wisconsindot.gov/Pages/dmv/dlr-agents/busns-lcnse/salvage-buyer-id.aspx)

**E-2.** *Primary source, New York — cost boundary.* New York's salvage vehicle examination costs **$200** with a NY State Salvage Certificate as proof of ownership and **$205** without. The examination's stated purpose is to determine whether a rebuilt salvage vehicle is stolen or contains stolen parts. Arriving more than 30 minutes after the scheduled appointment costs another **$150** and a rescheduled exam; arriving on illegal plates or registration can get the buyer ticketed and the **vehicle held by DMV** until legal transport is arranged. These are process failure modes with direct, doc

**B-1.** *Failure mode.* "Always inspect before you bid" is only partially available at a salvage auction. At Copart preview, a buyer may open the hood and photograph the vehicle, but **may not test drive it, may not start it themselves, and may not bring tools of any kind, including OBD-II diagnostic code readers**, into the yard. The inspection that the best practice assumes — a compression test, a scan for stored fault codes, a drive — is structurally unavailable. <https://autosxpert.com/can-you-test-drive-cars-at-copart/> · <https://autosxpert.com/can-i-look-at-cars-at-copart/> **[secondar

**C-5.** *Disaster-cycle boundary condition.* After major floods, NICB repeatedly warns that flood-damaged vehicles enter the resale market; insured total losses are retitled with a flood brand, but uninsured and title-washed units are not, and some are cleaned up, moved out of state, and retitled with no indication of damage. NICB's free VINCheck covers only vehicles reported stolen or declared salvage/total-loss by **participating NICB member insurers**, covering more than 92 percent of the market — i.e. it also has a defined, non-zero blind spot. An individual buyer's post-hurricane risk is

11. DOJ warns individual buyers of a specific failure mode: a clean-looking result may be a false negative. The consumer page states that "more than half of the states report data to the system," warns of a "false negative indication, such as 'no junk or salvage history,'" and notes that "brand washing can occur if the motor vehicle is retitled in another state." (https://vehiclehistory.bja.ojp.gov/nmvtis_consumers)

**In scope.** The internal mechanism of the practice itself: what an individual (non-dealer, non-dismantler) buyer must do, in what order, to buy a vehicle at a US salvage auction and end up with a legally titled, usable vehicle at a predictable cost. That includes the access/eligibility gate, the information the buyer can and cannot obtain before bidding, the bidding mechanism, the total-landed-cost model, the post-sale payment/pickup clock, and the state re-titling gate. Also in scope: the invariants that hold across every salvage auction, and the limits at which the practice stops protectin

39. Title type is the single highest-consequence pre-bid variable. Copart: "Ownership Documents… Each type carries certain ownership rights, restrictions and burdens. Research each title type to ensure its viability for your intended use of the lot" — https://www.copart.ca/content/us/en-ca/pdfs/newmemberguide_en.pdf (p. 15). 40. Non-repairable / certificate-of-destruction lots are terminal: such a vehicle is declared non-repairable under state law and cannot be rebuilt, retitled or legally driven again, though it may remain exportable or saleable for parts — https://cartitles.com/certificate-o

57. Inspection cannot see flood or progressive corrosion damage. Senate testimony on salvage/flood fraud records that flood damage to electronics and structural corrosion develops over time and remains invisible to casual inspection — https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CHRG-109shrg65005/html/CHRG-109shrg65005.htm. 58. Title brands can be laundered across states. NMVTIS exists to stop this, but the statutory gap is explicit: states are required to perform an inquiry before titling an out-of-state vehicle, yet "neither the Anti Car Theft Act nor its implementing regulations require states to ch

**B-3.** *Failure mode: over-reading the condition label.* Copart's "Run and Drive" means only that **at the time the vehicle arrived at the yard**, Copart verified it started, went into gear, and moved forward under its own power. Copart attaches no guarantee that the vehicle is roadworthy, that it may be driven lawfully on any highway, or that it will still start or move at pickup — deterioration and battery discharge between arrival and pickup are explicitly contemplated. The disclaimer places the burden of ascertaining condition entirely on the buyer. <https://blog.autobidmaster.com/2022/0

**B-4.** The gap in B-3 is not hypothetical: consumer-law question threads document buyers who purchased on a Run-and-Drive designation and received a vehicle whose engine did not run on inspection. This is a recurring, not isolated, complaint pattern. <https://www.justanswer.com/consumer-protection-law/mv4i2-bought-car-copart-run-drive-status.html> **[secondary — anecdotal; treat as existence proof of the failure mode, not as a rate]**

**E-1.** *Primary source, Virginia.* A Virginia rebuilt examination requires the buyer to bring proof of a passed Virginia state inspection, the LES 022A request form, **receipts for any original parts**, **a photograph of the vehicle before the repairs**, and old component parts displaying the VIN where applicable; the exam fee is **$125** plus a **$15** substitute title fee. The before-repair photograph is the trap: a buyer who does not photograph the vehicle *before* touching it has already failed a requirement that cannot be satisfied retroactively. <https://www.dmv.virginia.gov/vehicles/t

**E-3.** *Spread.* Rebuilt-inspection fees vary by roughly an order of magnitude across states — reported at $10 in Montana, $25 in Missouri, $40 in Florida, $50 in Arizona, $65 in Texas, against New York's $200. A "typical rebuilt inspection cost" carried across state lines is a modeling error. <https://carregistrationfee.com/articles/salvage-rebuilt-title-registration.html> **[secondary — cross-check against the two primary DMV sources above, which corroborate the high end]**

**A-3.** *Failure mode: registering into the wrong tier.* At IAA locations in Michigan and Utah, public buyers are restricted to **Clear Title** vehicles only, so most salvage inventory at those yards is invisible-but-unbuyable to a registered public buyer. A buyer who registers, pays the membership fee, and then discovers the inventory is off-limits has paid for access they cannot use. IAA public-buyer registration itself requires a government photo ID showing signature and residence address plus a $225 annual membership fee. <https://help.iaai.com/s/article/IAA-Public-Buyer-Guidelines-159051

**D-3.** Financing is a separate and generally tighter constraint than insurance: lenders may decline to finance branded-title vehicles, which forces a cash purchase. For an individual buyer this converts a nominally cheap vehicle into a large undiversified cash outlay. <https://www.helpforlemoncars.com/blog/2024/11/are-salvage-and-rebuild-titles-worth-the-risk-what-to-know-about-them/> **[secondary]**

**F-2.** *Time-pressure failure mode.* Payment is due within **3 business days including the day of sale**, with a **$50 per vehicle** late fee, and storage begins if the vehicle is not collected within **3 days of auction including sale day**, at a reported **$20–$50 per day**. An individual buyer without pre-arranged funds and pre-arranged transport is on a clock that a dealer with a floor plan and a house hauler is not. <https://vininfohub.com/copart-fees-explained> · <https://carsfromwest.com/en/copart-fees> **[secondary]**

**F-5.** *Underestimated repair category.* Airbag/restraint module replacement and ADAS recalibration are reported as the costs individual buyers most often omit, with ADAS work cited as capable of exceeding 35 percent of a repair bill. These are also precisely the systems a preview inspection cannot assess (**B-1**, **B-2**) — the largest cost uncertainty sits in the blind spot. <https://www.amerifreight.net/auto-shipping/salvage-bid-auctions-tips-best-practices> **[secondary]**

52. **Bidder-verifies-everything.** Across Copart, IAA and broker terms, every representation on the lot page is seller-supplied or point-in-time, and the contract assigns verification to the buyer. This is the concept's central invariant; nearly every best practice is a workaround for it. 53. **All clocks run against the buyer.** Deposit must precede bidding; payment is due in 2–3 business days; storage starts within days of sale; the seller's approval window (On Approval) is one business day and binds only the buyer. None of these can be extended after the fact. 54. **Title type dominates pr

**Disconfirming sources were sought and found.** Claims 57–63 come from sources that undercut the premise that diligent buyer practice controls the risk: the Senate hearing record on salvage/flood fraud, NHTSA's 2026 airbag-inflator alert, AAMVA's description of the NMVTIS statutory gap, and the insurability and resale-value limits. These are reported as limits of the concept, not softened.

**C21. ⚠ Insurance is a gating risk, not an afterthought, and can be refused outright.** TxDMV warns that "often rebuilt vehicles are denied insurance. Check with your insurance agent before purchasing the vehicle," and that "rebuilt vehicles can cause problems that will cost more to repair than the actual value of the vehicle." This undercuts the naïve savings case: a car that cannot be comprehensively insured or legally registered has no usable value to an individual buyer regardless of the hammer price.

**B-2.** *Boundary condition on the fallback.* The recommended substitute — a third-party pre-purchase inspector — inherits the same constraints: inspectors are generally not permitted to test drive auction vehicles, and are not permitted to jump-start a vehicle with a dead battery themselves. A remote inspection therefore cannot disconfirm a drivetrain fault; it can only confirm visible damage, fluids, and body/frame condition. <https://www.carinspector.us/services/66-auction-pre-purchase-inspections> **[secondary]**

13. Airbags are the salvage-specific safety risk with an official federal warning behind it. On September 23, 2024, the National IPR Center, HSI, CBP, NHTSA and the Automotive Anti-Counterfeiting Council launched the "Put the Brakes on Fakes" campaign, warning that "dangerous, substandard aftermarket airbags can, and have, injured and killed people in otherwise survivable crashes," and advising owners of used vehicles with unknown crash history to arrange an airbag inspection by a qualified mechanic. (https://www.ice.gov/news/releases/automotive-safety-awareness-campaign-warns-consumers-about-

The emphasis is on **boundary conditions** (where a stated best practice stops applying), **failure modes** (how the practice fails in the field), **disagreements** between sources, and **disconfirming evidence** against the common advice. Jurisdiction is the United States unless noted.

**U-2. How restricted is public access, really?** Aggregator sources give a clean split between no-license and broker-required states (<https://blog.autobidmaster.com/2026/06/auto-auction-licensing-requirement/>), but practitioner discussion reports the picture is messier in practice, with buyers in nominally title-lax states still uncertain whether a broker is required (<https://grassrootsmotorsports.com/forum/grm/copart-auctions-in-a-very-title-lax-state-do-i-still-need-a-broker/201061/page1/>). No authoritative state-by-state primary source was located; the IAA official page was reachable o

**C7. A brokered purchase adds a second fee layer on top of the auction's.** The broker terms set a transaction fee of "$250.00 or 5% of the vehicle Sale Price (whatever is higher) not including Auctions fees, for each vehicle purchased," a transportation assistance fee of "$75.00 plus the cost of transportation" that "cannot be refunded regardless if the order is cancelled," and a $50.00 late payment fee.

**C10. The auction's own condition data is contractually disclaimed, so it cannot be the basis of a bid.** Copart's member terms state "ALL VEHICLES ARE SOLD 'AS-IS WHERE-IS,' WITHOUT ANY WARRANTY, EXPRESS OR IMPLIED," that "Members shall not rely on Vehicle Information in deciding whether or how much to bid," and that "it is the sole responsibility of the Member to ascertain, confirm, research, inspect, and/or investigate vehicles." The broker terms extend the disclaimer explicitly to "year, make, model, condition, ACV, damage amount, damage type, drivability, accessories, mileage, odometer d

**C16. Bids are irrevocable and the high bid may still be rejected, so bid discipline is asymmetric.** "Once a bid has been submitted, it cannot be retracted, deleted, or cancelled. All bids are final and binding," and it is "the Buyer's responsibility to understand when they are highest bidder to avoid bidding against him/herself," with the buyer "required to pay winning bid amount even if the Buyer bids against him/herself." Separately, "On-Approval" vehicles are not released "unless and until the auction notifies Company and Buyer of its acceptance of the high bid," decided by 6:00 PM PST t

3. **Copart's and IAA's own current public-buyer rules could not be read directly.** Copart's licensing, member-fee, and security-deposit pages render client-side and returned no text to automated retrieval; IAA's auction-rules and help pages returned bot-detection interstitials or a TLS error. Consequently the deposit and fee figures in C5, C7, and C8 come from a **Copart-hosted third-party broker's** buyer terms dated 2024-04-22, not from Copart's own published schedule. They are representative of brokered buying, and the broker layer itself adds cost; a direct Copart Basic/Premier member wo

**D-2. Disconfirming, with a hard boundary.** The insurability claim in D-1 applies to *rebuilt* titles, not *salvage* titles. A salvage-titled vehicle cannot be legally driven until rebuilt and retitled, and rarely qualifies for collision or comprehensive coverage in that state. The distinction between the two brands is the single highest-leverage fact for an individual buyer, and much popular advice collapses them. <https://www.quote.com/auto-insurance/rebuilt-vs-salvage-title/> · <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vehicle_title_branding> **[secondary]**

**D-4.** Reported resale-value penalties diverge by brand: roughly **20–40 percent** below a clean title for a *rebuilt* vehicle, versus **50–80 percent** for a vehicle carrying the damage history as salvage. The exit price, not the entry price, is where the individual buyer's margin is decided. <https://www.carinsurance.com/value-rebuilt-title-vs-clean-title.aspx> · <https://appraisalengine.com/company/salvage-title-vs-rebuilt-title-vehicle-value/> **[secondary]**

1. An individual's eligibility to bid on a *salvage* lot is set by the law of the state where the **vehicle** is located, not where the buyer lives; Copart's own licensing overview tabulates eligibility per state and per buyer type ("Dealers/Dismantlers", "General Businesses and Exporters", "Private Individuals"), with separate columns for titled items and salvage items — https://www.copart.ca/content/us/en-ca/pdfs/newmemberguide_en.pdf (p. 7). 2. In that same table, private individuals are marked **BROKER** (i.e. cannot buy directly) for salvage in a large block of states including California

7. Physical preview is allowed and free, but only during business hours: Copart tells members they "can preview all Copart vehicles at no cost, Monday through Friday, during regular business hours" — https://www.copart.ca/content/us/en-ca/pdfs/newmemberguide_en.pdf (p. 8). 8. The preview is deliberately shallow. Copart's yard rules state: "As a safety precaution, please do not attempt to start a vehicle without a Copart employee," and "**Tools of any kind, including diagnostic code readers, are not allowed in the yard**" — https://www.copart.ca/content/us/en-ca/pdfs/newmemberguide_en.pdf (p. 1

1. **Payment deadline: 2 vs. 3 business days.** Copart's member guide says three business days including the sale date (https://www.copart.ca/content/us/en-ca/pdfs/newmemberguide_en.pdf p. 12); the Copart-hosted broker agreement says two working days (https://www.copart.com/content/us/en/pdfs/terms%20&%20conditions_01082020.pdf p. 2). Both are primary. The likeliest reconciliation is that the broker imposes a stricter deadline than the platform, but no source states that explicitly. The individual buyer at a salvage auction is, by definition, the inexperienced party bidding against repeat professionals — a structural disadvantage that no checklist of "best practices" removes. <https://research.upjohn.org/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?filename=4&article=1176&context=up_press&type=additional>

**G-1.** In common-value auctions the winner is the bidder with the most optimistic estimate of the asset and therefore tends to overestimate and overpay — the winner's curse. A salvage vehicle, whose true repair cost is unknown to all bidders, is close to a textbook common-value good. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winner%27s_curse>

**G-4.** Field evidence from online auctions ("The Bidder's Curse", Malmendier & Lee) shows bidders paying above a simultaneously available fixed price for identical goods — overbidding survives outside the laboratory.
